summary:
Chandīgarh, a union territory of India, is assessed at the national score: the country review identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02). A visitor therefore stands under India's national framework as it stands after the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill passed both houses of Parliament on 25 March 2026, with presidential assent still pending.

The amendment removes the self-identification right affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment and confines legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme altogether. Critics warn that the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people; India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Recognition is conditioned on medical certification. The bill makes medical-board and district-authority certification mandatory for gender-affirming surgery, which converts identity documentation into a clinical process for any trans traveller whose papers rest on that certification. The bill also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' anyone to be transgender, amending the 2019 law. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people, and rights activists among them Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. The government presents the bill as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; the bill was passed amid protests in Mumbai.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment reverses a recognition model that had held since the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling and that the 2019 statute had codified, so documents issued before the amendment rest on a legal basis the bill withdraws. Whether existing identity documents remain valid once assent is given is not addressed in the sources.

The government's stated rationale, wider access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, sits against the assessment of rights groups that the scheme's categories exclude the majority of people who self-identify as trans, non-binary or gender-fluid. The People's Union for Civil Liberties frames the new coercion offences as a return to colonial-era criminalisation rather than as an added safeguard.

Country-level reporting on police treatment of LGBT+ people is comparatively restrained: the UK Home Office's December 2025 note describes abuse as limited and not systemic, with a higher likelihood in conservative rural areas. Documented incidents of mistreatment nonetheless cluster in exactly the settings a traveller passes through, namely railway stations, airport terminals and passport offices.

India's estimated two million transgender people give the recognition scheme a large affected population, and the March 2026 passage was contested in public, with protests reported in Mumbai.
localsOnly:
Residents of Chandīgarh are governed by the same national recognition scheme as visitors: legal recognition is limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and to intersex people, with medical-board and district-authority certification required for gender-affirming surgery. Self-identification alone no longer suffices once the amendment is assented.

The government presents the amended framework as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Residents who fall outside the recognised categories may find that scheme eligibility follows the certification route rather than self-declaration.

Since the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita took effect in 2024, the gender-identity-specific offences of the Indian Penal Code that had shielded trans people from sexual violence no longer apply, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Police conduct is governed in part by court direction. The Madras High Court's 7 June 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police require police sensitisation, ban conversion therapy, and direct the National Medical Commission and education authorities; they bind within that court's jurisdiction, and residents outside it rely on comparable intervention by their own high courts, which the sources describe as having acted repeatedly for trans and LGBT+ people.

Discrimination on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity, is barred, and same-sex acts are not criminal. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership remain unavailable to residents, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was pending at the time of the sources. Whether it has since been given, and whether any provisions were altered in the assent stage, is unresolved here.

No Chandīgarh-specific enforcement data appears in the inventory. There is no sourced reporting of checkpoint, police or document incidents within this union territory; the incidents cited come from other Indian states and are used as indicators of a national pattern.

Whether the March 2026 recognition scheme changes passport marker practice, visa screening or entry-decision practice for travellers entering or departing Chandīgarh is not sourced. The passport medical-examination requirement is documented through a single Allahabad High Court relief decision of February 2026 and its general applicability is unresolved.

The scope of the conversion-therapy ban and of the police sensitisation guidelines outside the Madras High Court's jurisdiction is not established by these sources. The UK Home Office note addresses police abuse of LGBT+ people generally rather than trans-specific mistreatment, and its December 2025 date precedes the March 2026 amendment.

Validity of identity documents issued before the amendment, and any transition arrangements for people already certified, are not addressed in the inventory.
